Titolo: Briefing: Libyan rival institutions agree on election roadmap
Eventi: At a glance: (1) Libya's key governing institutions announced on 18 June that they agreed on a roadmap to bring the country's transitional phase to an end; (2) Presidential and parliamentary elections should be held no later than 17 February 2027, according to the agreement; (3) Meanwhile, the eastern-based Libyan National Army said that it backed a separate US-led initiative to unify executive power before elections. The Tripoli-based Presidential Council and High Council of State (HCS) and the east-based House of Representatives (HoR) made the announcement on 18 June, noting their agreement on a principles document aimed at ending the transitional phase. They said in a joint statement that the polls should be held simultaneously no later than 17 February 2027 based on the 6+6 electoral laws and the 13th constitutional amendment. The roadmap provides for a sovereign committee to oversee the electoral process, including the Governor of the Central Bank of Libya and the chairman of HNEC, plus representatives from the security sector and the 5+5 Joint Military Commission. The document also includes measures on oil revenues, frozen assets, oversight of natural resources and a unified budget. The LNA issued a statement expressing support for a separate US-led initiative to unify executive power before elections.

Titolo: Trump adviser pushes power-sharing plan for oil-rich Libya
Eventi: Massad Boulos, an adviser to US President Donald Trump on the Middle East and Africa, told the FT that he was working to bring the country's fragmented institutions under a single authority while encouraging US oil groups to invest. "Our plan is to have one unified government and to unify all the institutions,‚Äù said Boulos, a Lebanese-American businessman who is father-in-law to Tiffany, the US president's daughter. Washington, said Boulos, had been encouraging US oil majors to invest in Libya, noting that ConocoPhillips and Chevron had already signed agreements with Libya in 2026. Boulos said his plan would be "complementary‚Äù to UN efforts to hold parliamentary elections and could end up as "part of a package‚Äù and a "short-term arrangement‚Äù preceding parliamentary and presidential polls. The plan would place Saddam Haftar, son of Khalifa Haftar the warlord who controls eastern Libya, at the head of an executive presidential council, according to people familiar with the matter. They added that Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh, prime minister since 2021 of the UN-recognised government in Tripoli in western Libya, would remain in his post, while a close relative would occupy a national security post. Saddam Haftar is chief of staff of the ground forces of the self-styled Libyan National Army, the armed faction his father commands. In Haftar's fiefdom in eastern Libya no dissent is tolerated and human rights groups allege that brutal methods have been used to silence opponents. Dbeibeh's tenure as prime minister is protected by a patchwork of aligned armed groups, some of which have been accused by UN bodies of crimes including torture, illegal detention and human trafficking in migrants.

Titolo: EU Parliament approves 'strictest-ever' migration law
Eventi: On 17 June 2026 the European Parliament gave the final green light to a new EU law allowing controversial return hubs outside the bloc and home searches, as conservatives voted with far-right groups to pass the legislation. It allows EU countries to set up deportation centres outside the bloc (return hubs), through agreements with non-EU countries. Only unaccompanied minors would be exempt from the measure. The legislation raises the maximum legal detention period for irregular migrants from six months to two years, with a possible six-month extension and an unlimited duration for persons considered as posing a security risk. Entry bans would rise from five to ten years in most cases, with lifetime bans possible for security risks. Deportations are no longer automatically suspended while legal challenges are pending.

Titolo: EU migrant 'return hubs'- explained
Eventi: On March 9, 2026, the Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs (LIBE) in the EU Parliament approved amendments to a proposal by the European Commission to overhaul EU return procedures. This return regulation, first proposed by the Commission in March 2025, would streamline the return process of rejected asylum seekers across the EU. While the details of how these proposed return hubs would function remain unclear, the proposal establishes the following criteria: (1) EU states can only establish hubs in non-EU countries meeting international human rights standards, including non-refoulement (prohibiting returns to persecution). (2) EU states would need to sign a bilateral agreement with the host country. These must detail transfer procedures, living conditions, and stay durations, with monitoring mechanisms to track implementation and adapt to changing circumstances in host countries. (3) The proposal initially excluded unaccompanied minors and families with children from being sent to return hubs, but the Council's December 2025 agreement overturned this for families -- now permitting their transfer to hubs alongside adults.(4) The Council approach confirms hubs serve dual roles: final destinations or transit centers for onward deportation, raising concerns about the length of detention in these facilities.

Valutazioni: [MIG] The origins of the new regulation go back to the 2008 Return Directive (Directive 2008/115/EC), which set basic minimum standards across EU countries for handling people without legal permission to stay -- including a six-month detention limit, preference for voluntary departure, and procedures largely left to member states.. Unlike the old directive, this is a full "regulation" -- directly applying across the EU without national tweaks, allowing for new approaches by member states to enable returns to non-EU countries. Although it is separate, it fits into the logic of the broader EU Migration Pact, which will take full effect in June 2026, with the goal of creating a "common European system" for returns. Return hubs are physical centers in non-EU countries where people with rejected asylum claims would be sent to await deportation. The goal is to speed up deportations by processing returns in third countries rather than inside the EU -- part of a major push to raise current low return rates. Only about 20 to 30 percent of roughly 700,000 annual return orders are currently enforced. They operate via bilateral agreements between EU states and host governments, with no overarching EU-wide binding framework -- just promises of compliance with basics like non-refoulement. Italy's deal with Albania to build and run centers in Sh‡´ngjin and Gjader -- 670 million euros over five years to process 36,000 people annually -- serves as the main blueprint.

Titolo: Explainer Why are Libya's western authorities at odds
Eventi: Despite reunification efforts, Libya's east and west still operate under rival authorities, often backed by international actors. However, negotiations around reunification, led by the UN Mission in Libya (Unsmil), have recently gained momentum. Libyan commentators widely note that the talks coincide with Washington's "renewed interest" in Libya, with some accusing the US of pursuing a "rival" track. While the talks have been cautiously welcomed by all sides, divisions persist over what that process should ultimately entail. Libya's capital Tripoli, in the west, hosts the internationally recognised Government of National Unity (GNU), the advisory High Council of State (HCS) and the Presidential Council (PC). The PC chairman acts as the internationally recognised head of state and supreme commander of Libya's western army (a title contested by the eastern authorities). The country's legislature, the House of Representatives (HoR), is based in the eastern city of Tobruk. The HoR formed the Government of National Stability (GNS), a rival to the UN-recognised GNU. The HoR and the GNS are backed by the powerful east-based Libyan National Army (LNA) and its strongman, Khalifa Haftar. The current UN-sponsored talks are split into three tracks. Negotiations for the first track, focused on economic unification, started on 6 April. This resulted in an economic agreement and unified budget between the rival authorities. Central Bank of Libya (CBL) Governor Naji Issa said it would be "pivotal in ending financial division and enhancing economic stability" in the country. A Unsmil spokesperson told Libyan media that discussions would continue over governance and security cooperation the following week, before final talks over national reconciliation and human rights the week after. Libyan media have widely reported on what they see as renewed interest from the US. Political analyst Mohamed Tantoush told pro-eastern media outlets in April that the US was proposing "parallel" plans for unification that did not "intersect significantly" with the UN proposals. Libyan commentators, especially in the east, see the US plans as more military-focused and "pragmatic". Washington's revived interest in Libya appears to have been intensified by the energy disruption caused by the Iran war. Prior to this, in January, US company ConocoPhillips secured a 25-year contract with Libya's Waha Oil Company, after withdrawing years prior due to political instability. Libya holds 3% of the world's proven oil reserves, amounting to 48 billion barrels. Before the war, US presidential adviser Massad Boulos hailed "the growing bilateral energy partnership" between the two countries.

Titolo: Migration Trends at Libya's Borders (October - December 2025)
Eventi: Following a seasonal peak in the third quarter of 2025, the fourth quarter recorded a sharp 44 per cent decline in overall inflows to Libya. This downturn is attributed to several factors. Primarily, a broader stagnation within the national labour market, driven by the conclusion of agricultural harvests and the year- end slowdown of construction projects, reduced the demand for migrant labour across multiple municipalities. This was further compounded by increased anti- smuggling law enforcement operations and seasonal weather constraints. Social media monitoring corroborated an uptick in anti- smuggling operations, while Mediterranean crossings became particularly perilous due to winter sea conditions. These conditions restricted the operations of migration facilitators and resulted in fewer crossing attempts; nevertheless, coastal field teams continued to report boat capsizing incidents during these months. Despite this general downward trend, arrivals via the South-West borders of Chad and Niger increased by 14 per cent. This surge was not a result of increased labour demand, but rather a tactical response to escalating insecurity and intensified conflict along the South-East corridor. As traditional routes became impassable or too dangerous, Sudanese nationals were increasingly likely to reroute through Chad or Niger to enter Libya, highlighting the high degree of adaptability and vulnerability inherent in current regional migration flows to Libya. Over 87 per cent of migrants originated from Libya's six neighbouring countries, with Egyptians (33%), Nigeriens (31%), and Chadians (10%) forming the largest groups. Sudanese nationals accounted for 8 per cent, Tunisians 5 per cent, and Algerians 1 per cent. Among migrants from non‚Äëneighbouring countries, the main nationalities were Nigerians (5%), Malians (4%) and Burkinabe (3%).

Repsol began drilling the A1-2/130 (Muammal Nsr) exploration well on 31 December 2024, in the country's southwest, 12 km from Libya's largest oil field, Sharara, as reported by Reuters. The well is slated to be drilled to a depth of 1844 m (6,050 ft). It is one of six wells in Repsol's NC115 and NC186 license areas in the southwestern Murzuq basin that the company was scheduled to drill when it announced a resumption of its exploration activities in April in a news release. Akakus, a joint venture of NOC in partnership with Repsol, TotalEnergies, OMV, and Equinor, operates the Sharara oil field which the partners hope to ramp up to a targeted 260,000 BOPD. Sharara's production capacity is 320,000 B/D, according to Zacks Investment Research.

Titolo: Turkey expands grip in Libya
Eventi: The Turkish military operates in various Libyan locations including the Joint Ground Training and Exercise Center in Tajoura and the Special Forces Center in Al-Khums. Turkish forces are also present at key airbases like Al-Watiya, Misrata and Mitiga. In total around 3,000 Turkish personnel are currently deployed in Libya comprising over 2,000 TAF soldiers and approximately 800 private military contractors from the Turkish company SADAT. Additionally up to 50 Turkish intelligence operatives (MIT) are believed to be active on Libyan soil. Turkeys focus is primarily on training the forces loyal to the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU). Ankaras support extends to supplying military equipment like Bayraktar TB2 drones, T-155 Firtina howitzers and Hawk air defense systems. Ankara maintains a permanent naval presence off the Libyan coast with two warships patrolling the waters near Tripoli. The logistical support network is bolstered by an estimated 280 cargo flights conducted by Turkish C-130 and A400 transport aircraft circumventing Greek airspace to reach Tripoli.
